rows.speaker: Gm
rows.claim: Gm's mutawātir form doubles yāʾ in mayyitan, a fuller adjective alongside maytan; both mean dead or lifeless, with greater phonetic weight.
rows.anchor: Variant with doubled yāʾ gives fuller adjective mayyitan beside standard maytan; semantic field remains dead/lifeless

rows.speaker: Pss
rows.claim: Pss's canonical active reading changes passive 'you are brought forth' to active or intransitive 'you come forth,' shifting agency while retaining kh-r-j.
rows.anchor: shifting emergence agency while keeping kh-r-j

rows.speaker: Cs
rows.claim: Cs's mutawātir reading deletes hamza, simplifying raʾā to raytum in a common Ḥijāzī practice.
rows.anchor: Hamza deletion — raʾā simplified to raytum, common Ḥijāzī practice

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The hmz mutawātir reading softens hamza, producing an intermediate form between full hamza and deletion.
rows.anchor: Hamza softening — intermediate between full hamza and deletion

rows.speaker: madd
rows.claim: The madd mutawātir reading lengthens the vowel before hamza, giving the word a deliberative prosody.
rows.anchor: Madd extension — lengthened vowel before hamza creates deliberative prosody

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: The vw reading shifts mīm from kasra to ḍamma: mutnā follows the u-stem māta/yamūtu pattern, standard in Ḥijāz, while mitnā follows the alternative a-stem pattern.
rows.anchor: Form I māta has two conjugation patterns — māta/yamūtu with u-stem and māta/yamātu with a-stem

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: The vw form has doubled yāʾ (mayyitan) rather than contracted maytan; grammarians debate whether mayyit is currently dying and mayt already dead.
rows.anchor: Vowel-length variant: mayyitan (with tashdīd on yāʾ) vs standard maytan

rows.speaker: skn
rows.claim: The skn reading places ḍamma on sīn instead of sukūn, yielding fuller yusuran; it may reflect an archaic nominal pattern or dialectal variant.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: ḍamma on sīn instead of sukūn — yusuran vs yusran; a fuller vocalization

rows.speaker: Lvw
rows.claim: The Lvw singular kabīr replaces plural kabāʾir, shifting from major sins as a class to 'the great sin,' potentially one supreme sin.
rows.anchor: potentially identifying ONE supreme sin rather than a class of sins

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: This vw form of ummahāt replaces hamza with kasra on initial alif and has shadda on mīm with kasra, a dialectal form for mothers.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift on ummahāt: hamza replaced by kasra on initial alif

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: This vw variant has kasra on initial alif and fatḥa on doubled mīm, another dialectal pronunciation of ummahāt.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant: kasra on initial alif with fatḥa on doubled mīm — another dialectal pronunciation of ummahāt

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: This vw variant has kasra on alif and mīm; it is a dialectal pronunciation affecting the initial syllable, with no semantic shift.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant on ummahāt: kasra on alif + kasra on mīm — dialectal pronunciation affecting the initial syllable only, no semantic shift

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: This vw dialectal form has kasra on alif and fatḥa on mīm; the meaning 'mothers' is unchanged.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant: kasra on alif + fatḥa on mīm — another dialectal form; the semantic content (mothers) is unchanged

rows.speaker: Lvw
rows.claim: The Lvw vocalization reads Ibrāhām instead of Ibrāhīm, replacing long ī with ā as a phonological adaptation of the foreign name; both are canonical.
rows.anchor: Variant vocalization: Ibrāhām instead of Ibrāhīm — the long ā replaces the long ī

rows.speaker: Lvw
rows.claim: The elongated nashāʾa with alif-madd and shorter nashʾa are both canonical; the longer form may stress an extended process rather than a punctual event.
rows.anchor: The elongated form may emphasize the process (extended duration of the act) vs the punctual event

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The hmz form drops hamza, reading qurāna for qurʾāna through tashīl, in keeping with Ḥijāzī norms that lighten or elide hamza.
rows.anchor: Without hamza — reads qurāna instead of qurʾāna; the hamza is dropped (tashīl)

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The hmz reading softens the second hamza by replacing it with vowel lengthening; standard Ḥafṣ retains both hamzas.
rows.anchor: Hamza softening: second hamza replaced by vowel lengthening; standard Ḥafṣ retains both hamzas

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The hmz variant replaces hamza with alif-madd, further smoothing the double-hamza sequence.
rows.anchor: Hamza replaced by alif madd — further phonetic smoothing of the double-hamza sequence

rows.speaker: Cs
rows.claim: The Cs reading completely deletes hamza through tashīl; this attested canonical form removes the glottal interruption.
rows.anchor: Complete hamza deletion (tashīl) — attested canonical variant; reduces the glottal interruption entirely

rows.speaker: Imp
rows.claim: The Imp form yakhfī is masculine singular instead of feminine takhfā; it can make Allāh the implicit subject: He will hide no secret from you.
rows.anchor: Masculine 3rd person singular yakhfī instead of feminine takhfā — verb becomes masculine

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The hmz reading drops hamza between vowels, changing qurʾān to qurān with phonetic smoothing but no semantic change.
rows.anchor: Hamza dropped: qurʾān → qurān; simplification of hamza between vowels — no semantic change but phonetic smoothing

rows.speaker: skn
rows.claim: The skn reading places sukūn on lām for a lighter pronunciation; the meaning of the fraction is unchanged.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on lām — lighter pronunciation, same meaning; variant vocalization of the fraction

rows.speaker: CE
rows.claim: The CE genitive niṣfihi is coordinated with thuluthayī, so both are governed by min: 'less than two-thirds and its half and its third.'
rows.anchor: Genitive reading — niṣfihi as maʿṭūf on thuluthayī (both governed by min), restructures

rows.speaker: CE
rows.claim: The CE genitive thuluthihi parallels the niṣfihi variant; both are governed by min through thuluthayī.
rows.anchor: Genitive reading — parallel to niṣfihi variant, both governed by min through thuluthayī

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The hmz canonical variant drops hamza in Qurāni for Qurʾāni, removing the glottal stop.
rows.anchor: Hamza dropped — Qurāni instead of Qurʾāni; attested canonical variant removing glottal stop

rows.speaker: Pss
rows.claim: The Pss passive participle makes the herd frightened, driven out, or made to flee, rather than actively taking fright.
rows.anchor: Canonical passive participle reading shifts the herd from actively taking fright to being frightened, driven out, or made to flee

rows.speaker: Imp
rows.claim: The Imp reading changes imperfect prefix tu- to yu-, shifting from direct second-person address to a report about them.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant changes the imperfect prefix from second person tu- to third person yu-

rows.speaker: Imp
rows.claim: The Imp variant changes imperfect prefix ta- to ya-, shifting from direct plural address to third-person report while retaining root w-dh-r and object al-ākhirata.
rows.anchor: The variant changes the imperfect prefix from ta- to ya-, shifting from direct second-person plural address to third-person plural report

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: The vw vowel reading shifts the imperfect stem from a to i while preserving ḥ-s-b semantics, marking a live recitation pattern.
rows.anchor: Canonical vowel reading shifts the imperfect stem vowel from a to i, preserving ḥ-s-b semantics

rows.speaker: Imp
rows.claim: The Imp feminine passive tumnā agrees with feminine nuṭfah rather than masculine maniyy, shifting the syntactic center of emission.
rows.anchor: Canonical feminine passive: agreement can shift from masculine مَنِيّ to feminine نُطْفَةً, changing the syntactic center of emission

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The hmz canonical reading elides hamza in qurʾān to yield Qurān, simplifying the glottal stop without altering meaning.
rows.anchor: Hamza elision: the hamza (ʾ) in qurʾān is dropped, yielding Qurān; canonical reading of some reciters

rows.speaker: HzT
rows.claim: The HzT performance variant eases or alters hamza at the opening ءَأَنتُمْ boundary without changing the pronoun, comparison, or word identity.
rows.anchor: Hamza-related performance eases or alters realization at the opening ءَأَنتُمْ boundary

rows.speaker: CE
rows.claim: The CE case or mood variant raises the final vowel, making the benefit clause sound more independent than tanfaʿahu.
rows.anchor: Canonical case/mood variant raises the final vowel, allowing the benefit clause to sound more independent

rows.speaker: Vr
rows.claim: The Vr Form II passive with shadda intensifies or distributes the action, making the records spread thoroughly, repeatedly, or one after another.
rows.anchor: Canonical Form II passive with shadda intensifies or distributes the action: the records are made to be spread thoroughly
